issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: The snake-related trigger is hard to link coherently to the rest of this sexual-assault profile. Other triggers and strategies center on emergency/police/location cues, while no threat, appraisal, or memory content connects to animals or snakes. This makes that item look clinically disconnected rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Compulsive cleaning can occur after sexual assault, but in this profile it is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. The active pattern strongly links triggers, threat, and negative appraisals to maladaptive strategies, yet the listed triggers/threats/appraisals point to hypervigilance, emergency/uniform cues, and situational avoidance rather than contamination, dirtiness, or washing/control themes. As selected here, the cleaning item appears insufficiently connected to the rest of the profile.

vignette: Tariq, a fifty-four-year-old American of Middle Eastern descent, had been fifty-two when the sexual assault occurred at the downtown municipal clinic. He remembered the exact sequence: the heavy door clicking shut, the male clerk's uniformed sleeve brushing his shoulder, and the quiet shift from waiting to being alone in the consultation room with the man. The violation was swift, and when he stepped out, an ambulance was already idling at the curb, its siren cutting through the afternoon air. His PCL-5 score of 77 reflected the quiet intensity of his days, which settled into a rhythm of caution. He held to the belief that what happened to him was deeply unfair and nothing had been done about it, and he was certain the event happened because of the way he had acted, how he had nodded too readily and allowed the man to take his lead. Over the following months, Tariq's daily routines organized themselves around specific triggers. He found himself constantly scanning the office corridors for signs of danger, his eyes moving from face to face, checking for military or police uniforms, badges, or even the leather holsters and metallic tools that fell into the category of weapons. When a male project manager asked him to stay behind after a code review, Tariq reacted as if he were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong. He had stopped going to the municipal clinic, and when he passed it, he crossed to the opposite sidewalk, keeping distance from the building's entrance. His occupation as a software engineer anchored his avoidance in a precise environment. He began declining meetings that required him to sit alone with senior men, preferring instead to remain in the open atrium or at his desk, flanked by the server racks and the steady hum of his dual monitors. He only felt safe in those very limited places, and his colleagues noticed the shift; he would check the time, murmur an excuse, and retreat, his coding work continuing steadily while he carefully managed his proximity to authority figures and any man who stood too close. Tariq's days were marked by a parallel stream of appraisals and bodily responses. He wore casual shirts to avoid the crisp lines of formal uniforms, and when security patrols or police officers moved through the lobby, he felt the old tension return, standing alongside his constant awareness of the environment. He was certain he would never be able to feel normal emotions again; the sharp highs of joy and the quiet lows of sadness had flattened into a steady, watchful hum. When sirens wailed on the highway, he would pause mid-sentence, his hand moving to his chest. When an ambulance passed his building, he would step outside to watch it, not because he needed to, but because he had to be sure it was just passing through. His single status had deepened into a quiet routine; without a partner to share the watch with him, he navigated the city alone, constantly measuring the male presence in his path against the memory of that clinic room. It was the cumulative weight of these habits that finally brought him to seek help. He had noticed that his work fractured when forced to sit with male clients in unfamiliar rooms, and that he was no longer comfortable walking past the municipal building without feeling the pull of that uncorrected injustice. He came to therapy hoping to understand why his body still sounded the alarm over ordinary sounds, and what might loosen the boundaries of the safety he had carefully constructed. He was afraid that without intervention, he would remain trapped in the narrow corridor between past violation and present watchfulness, never quite stepping into the world he used to know.
